definition: The neuron doctrine is the view, accepted in the late 19th century, that the nervous system operates through discrete cell-to-cell communication between individual nerve cells. It became a foundation for reductionist approaches that explain brain and behavior in terms of molecular and cellular mechanisms.

reasons: The packet does not define the “neuron doctrine” as a view about discrete cell-to-cell communication between individual nerve cells; it only mentions that reductionism analyses assume acceptance of the neuron doctrine in the late 19th century.

The definition’s claim that the neuron doctrine “became a foundation for reductionist approaches” is not explicitly stated in the packet; the packet says reductionism has been an assumption since acceptance of the neuron doctrine, but does not directly frame the neuron doctrine itself as the foundation.

The definition’s phrasing about “explaining brain and behavior in terms of molecular and cellular mechanisms” is only indirectly supported; the packet discusses a later focus on molecular and cellular mechanisms promoted by developments, but does not explicitly connect this focus as a direct consequence of the neuron doctrine.
